title: Exponential Growth and Decay Models
subject: AP Calculus AB
objectives: Recognize that dy/dt = ky models a quantity changing at a rate proportional to its size, with solution y = y₀e^(kt).
Interpret the parameters y₀ and k, and distinguish growth (k > 0) from decay (k < 0).
Use given data to solve for k and make predictions.
Apply the model to half-life and doubling-time problems.

sections.heading: The Most Important Differential Equation
sections.content:
A huge number of real processes share one feature: the rate at which a quantity changes is proportional to how much of it there is. The more bacteria in a dish, the faster the colony grows, because every cell divides. The more radioactive atoms in a sample, the faster atoms decay, because each one can decay independently. The more money in an account, the faster it earns interest. Every one of these is the differential equation dy/dt = ky.

You solved this equation by separation of variables in the previous lesson, and the result is the model that this whole lesson builds on:

  dy/dt = ky  ⟹  y = y₀e^(kt),

where y₀ is the amount at time t = 0 and k is the constant of proportionality. Because the solution is an exponential function, proportional-rate processes always produce exponential curves — that's why 'exponential growth' is a household phrase for anything that snowballs.

The sign of k decides everything about the shape. If k > 0, the exponent grows and y increases without bound: exponential *growth*. If k < 0, the exponent becomes more negative and y shrinks toward zero: exponential *decay*. This single model — three symbols, y₀, k, and t — describes population growth, radioactive decay, drug elimination from the bloodstream, compound interest, and more. Mastering it is among the highest-value things you can take from the differential-equations unit.

sections.heading: Reading the Parameters y₀ and k
sections.content:
In y = y₀e^(kt), each symbol has a concrete meaning, and interpreting them correctly is half the battle on word problems.

y₀ is the *initial amount* — the value of y when t = 0, since e^(k·0) = e⁰ = 1, making y(0) = y₀·1 = y₀. Whatever the quantity was at the starting time goes directly into y₀. Read the problem for the 'at time zero' value, or for a value you can shift to be time zero.

k is the *relative (proportional) rate of change* — how fast y grows or shrinks per unit of itself, per unit time. A positive k means growth and a negative k means decay; the larger |k| is, the faster the change. Importantly, k is a continuous rate constant, which is close to but not identical to a stated percentage rate for small rates; on the AP exam, when a problem says dy/dt = ky, you take k directly as given or solve for it from data, rather than translating a percentage.

You typically find k from data. If you know the quantity at two times, plug both into y = y₀e^(kt) to get an equation you can solve for k (usually by dividing to cancel y₀, then taking a natural log). Once y₀ and k are known, the model predicts y at any time, and you can also solve for the time t when y reaches a target value by isolating the exponential and taking a logarithm.

sections.heading: Solving a Growth or Decay Problem

steps.title: Write the model
steps.content: Recognize the proportional-rate language (or dy/dt = ky) and write y = y₀e^(kt).

steps.title: Identify y₀
steps.content: Use the amount at time t = 0 as y₀ (or shift the clock so a known time becomes t = 0).

steps.title: Solve for k from data
steps.content: Substitute a second known (time, amount) pair, divide out y₀, and take a natural log to solve for k.

steps.title: Answer the question
steps.content: Substitute t to predict an amount, or set y to a target and solve for t with a logarithm.

sections.heading: Population Growth From Two Data Points
sections.content:
A bacterial culture grows so that its rate of increase is proportional to its size. It starts with 500 cells, and after 2 hours there are 2000 cells. Find the model and predict the population after 5 hours.

Model: y = y₀e^(kt). Since the initial count is 500, y₀ = 500, so y = 500e^(kt).

Find k using y(2) = 2000:
  2000 = 500e^(2k)
  4 = e^(2k)
  ln 4 = 2k
  k = (ln 4)/2 = ln 2 ≈ 0.3466 per hour.

So y = 500e^((ln 2)t) (equivalently y = 500·2^(t/2), reflecting that the population doubles every 2 hours).

Predict at t = 5:
  y(5) = 500e^(5·0.3466) = 500e^(1.733) ≈ 500·5.657 ≈ 2828 cells.

The answer is about 2828 bacteria after 5 hours. Notice how dividing the two-point equation eliminated y₀ and isolated the exponential, after which a single natural log delivered k.

sections.heading: y₀ Is the Amount at t = 0, and k's Sign Matters
sections.content: Two frequent errors. First, y₀ must be the amount at t = 0; if a problem gives the amount at some other time, either treat that time as t = 0 or substitute it as a data point to solve for y₀ — don't blindly use whichever number appears first. Second, growth has k > 0 and decay has k < 0; for decay problems you should expect a negative k (e.g., k = −ln2/half-life), and getting a positive k for a decaying quantity signals an algebra error. Also keep k (a continuous rate constant) distinct from a stated percent change; on AB you take dy/dt = ky as the model and find k from the given data.

sections.question: A quantity follows y = y₀e^(kt) with y₀ = 100 and k = −0.2. This describes:
sections.explanation: Because k = −0.2 is negative, the exponent becomes more negative as t increases, so y = 100e^(−0.2t) shrinks toward zero — exponential decay. A positive k would give growth, and k = 0 would give a constant.

sections.heading: Half-Life and Doubling Time
sections.content:
Two especially useful quantities describe how fast an exponential process moves: the doubling time (for growth) and the half-life (for decay). Both are constants for a given k — the hallmark of exponential behavior is that the time to double (or to halve) is always the same, no matter where you start.

For decay, the *half-life* T is the time for the quantity to fall to half its value. Set y = y₀/2 in y = y₀e^(kt): y₀/2 = y₀e^(kT) gives 1/2 = e^(kT), so kT = ln(1/2) = −ln 2, and T = −(ln 2)/k. Since k < 0 for decay, T comes out positive. Equivalently, k = −(ln 2)/T, which is how you find the rate constant when a problem gives the half-life directly (as with carbon-14's half-life of 5730 years).

For growth, the *doubling time* T_d solves 2 = e^(kT_d), giving T_d = (ln 2)/k. In the bacteria example, k = ln 2 per hour gave a doubling time of (ln 2)/(ln 2) = 1... but recall there k was ln2 per hour only because the population doubled every 2 hours — the model y = 500·2^(t/2) shows the period of 2 directly. The recurring number ln 2 ≈ 0.693 appears in both formulas because halving and doubling are the natural 'factor of 2' events of exponential change. Recognizing that half-life and doubling time are fixed, and tied to k through ln 2, lets you move quickly between a rate constant and these intuitive time scales.

sections.heading: Radioactive Decay and Half-Life
sections.content:
A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the amount present and has a half-life of 10 years. If 80 grams are present now, how much remains after 25 years?

Model: y = y₀e^(kt) with y₀ = 80. Find k from the half-life T = 10:
  k = −(ln 2)/T = −(ln 2)/10 ≈ −0.0693 per year.

So y = 80e^(−0.0693t), or equivalently y = 80·(1/2)^(t/10), which shows the half-life of 10 directly.

After 25 years:
  y(25) = 80·(1/2)^(25/10) = 80·(1/2)^(2.5) = 80·(0.1768) ≈ 14.1 grams.

About 14.1 grams remain. As a sanity check, 25 years is 2.5 half-lives: after 10 years 40 g, after 20 years 20 g, and a bit more decay brings it to roughly 14 g — consistent with the calculation. Writing the model in the (1/2)^(t/T) form often makes half-life arithmetic faster than carrying e^(kt).

sections.heading: Growth vs. Decay at a Glance

sections.question: A substance has a half-life of 5 years. What is its decay constant k in the model y = y₀e^(kt)?
sections.explanation: From y₀/2 = y₀e^(5k), we get 1/2 = e^(5k), so 5k = ln(1/2) = −ln 2 and k = −(ln 2)/5. The constant is negative because the quantity is decaying.

sections.heading: Recognize the Model Instantly
sections.content: On the AP exam, the phrase 'the rate of change is proportional to the amount' (or an equation dy/dt = ky) should immediately trigger y = y₀e^(kt) — you don't need to re-derive it every time, though showing the separation step earns credit on a 'solve the differential equation' prompt. Then: y₀ is the t = 0 amount, find k from a second data point or from a given half-life/doubling time, and use logarithms to solve for an unknown time. Keep units consistent and watch the sign of k. The alternative forms y = y₀·2^(t/T_d) for doubling and y = y₀·(1/2)^(t/T) for half-life often simplify the arithmetic.

sections.heading: Beyond Pure Exponentials: Cooling and Limits to Growth
sections.content:
The model y = y₀e^(kt) is powerful precisely because so many systems obey dy/dt = ky, but understanding its boundaries shows both its reach and where richer models take over.

A close cousin appears in Newton's Law of Cooling: an object's temperature changes at a rate proportional to the *difference* between its temperature and the surroundings, dT/dt = k(T − T_s), where T_s is the ambient temperature. This isn't quite dy/dt = ky, but a simple substitution makes it one: let u = T − T_s, so du/dt = dT/dt = k(T − T_s) = ku. Now it's the familiar equation, with solution u = u₀e^(kt), i.e. T − T_s = (T₀ − T_s)e^(kt). So a hot coffee's temperature doesn't decay toward zero — it decays exponentially toward room temperature, approaching T_s rather than 0. The same exponential machinery, shifted by a constant, models cooling, warming, and any process that relaxes toward an equilibrium value. This shifting trick is exactly the kind of reasoning the AP exam rewards, and it's solvable with the separation method you already know.

The deeper limitation of pure exponential growth is that nothing grows forever. A bacterial colony eventually exhausts its food; a population hits the carrying capacity of its environment. Real growth often starts exponential and then levels off, producing an S-shaped curve described by the *logistic* differential equation dy/dt = ky(1 − y/M), where M is the carrying capacity. When y is small the (1 − y/M) factor is near 1 and growth looks exponential; as y approaches M the factor shrinks toward 0 and growth halts. (The full logistic model is a BC topic, but recognizing that exponential growth is the small-population approximation to it deepens your understanding of when y = y₀e^(kt) applies.)

The takeaway is that the exponential model is the foundational case — the right description whenever the rate is genuinely proportional to the amount and resources are unlimited — and it serves as the building block from which cooling models (shift by a constant) and logistic models (multiply by a saturating factor) are constructed. Few equations in all of mathematics describe as much of the real world from as little input as dy/dt = ky.

When a quantity's rate of change is proportional to its size, dy/dt = ky, the solution is y = y₀e^(kt): y₀ is the amount at t = 0 and k is the proportional rate (k > 0 growth, k < 0 decay). Find k from a second data point or from a half-life/doubling time, using ln. Half-life is −(ln 2)/k and doubling time is (ln 2)/k; equivalently y = y₀(1/2)^(t/T) for decay and y = y₀·2^(t/T_d) for growth.
